summary: Open-cab steel lookout on the Ute Mountain Indian Reservation, Montezuma County, Colorado. The register dates it 1945; no second source confirms that year.

facts.design: Open cab with no roof on a 22-foot steel tower
facts.agency: Bureau of Indian Affairs (cooperator: Ute Mountain Ute Agency)

access.note: On the Ute Mountain Indian Reservation, which is tribal land. The sources describe no public access.

events.note: Built field on the register; not confirmed by a second source

evidence.supports: register number US 876, CO 14 (same number on the FFLA list)
administered by the Bureau of Indian Affairs
on the Ute Mountain Indian Reservation; open cab with no roof
evidence.quote: Located on the Ute Mountain Indian Reservation, Soda Point Lookout is also an open cab design but with no roof.
The 22' steel tower has climbing steps once common on power poles.

evidence.supports: Montezuma County; crowsnest; standing; NHLR US 876
evidence.quote: Soda Point Montezuma 37.12861 -108.46667 Crowsnest Standing NHLR US 876, CO 14

notes_for_editor: The 1945 build year rests on the register alone. A search result summarised an FFLA Colorado page (firelookout.org/cohost-co/soda.html) as giving 1962, and quoted a 1962 Mesa Verde forestry report second-hand. That page returned 404 in our fetch and the report was not reached, so neither is cited. Please check before publishing; if confirmed, the build year and the story need revising. Coordinates conflict: the record uses the FFLA point 37.12861, -108.46667, and gives the register point as 37.07307, -108.27353, about 18 km apart; the register's coordinates were not in the text read, so this is not resolved. Kind: the record says platform, FFLA says Crowsnest, and the register describes an open cab on a 22-foot steel tower. Height is not recorded as height_m because the register does not say whether 22 feet runs to the cab floor. Staffing and current condition are unknown. Access is on tribal land with no contact given in the sources. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story previously called the Ute Mountain Ute Agency a 'tribal agency'; the register names it only as a cooperator, so the story now says just that.
